query: For boride-based components used in hot-dip aluminum-plating equipment, what single intervention could improve resistance to molten-aluminum corrosion? Formulate one hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains its mechanism, predicts the improvement relative to an appropriate baseline, defines the conditions under which it should remain effective, cites supporting prior evidence, and specifies a controlled experiment whose results could falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Pre-oxidizing the surface of boride-based components to form a dense, adherent alumina (Al2O3) scale will reduce molten-aluminum corrosion during hot-dip aluminum plating by forming a protective diffusion barrier.
generation.material_initial_state: Boride-based component produced by conventional methods that lacks a purposely formed protective oxide layer.
generation.intervention: Apply a controlled high-temperature pre-oxidation treatment in an oxygen‐rich atmosphere to deliberately form a thin, uniform alumina (Al2O3) layer on the surface.
generation.conditions: This treatment is designed to be effective during subsequent exposure to molten aluminum at a temperature typical for hot-dip plating over the duration of industrial processing. The preformed alumina must remain intact under moderate thermal cycling and mechanical contact expected in service.
generation.structural_mediator: The continuous, dense Al2O3 layer acting as a diffusion barrier between the underlying boride substrate and molten aluminum.
generation.mechanism: The preformed alumina scale is thermodynamically stable and chemically inert with respect to molten aluminum, thereby limiting reactive interdiffusion and dissolution of the boride substrate. It acts as a physical and chemical barrier that reduces the direct contact between aggressive molten aluminum and the boride material.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to untreated boride components, the pre-oxidized components should exhibit a significantly lower rate of mass loss, reduced oxide spallation or surface degradation, and improved overall longevity when immersed in molten aluminum during plating.
generation.baseline: Standard boride-based components used in hot-dip aluminum plating equipment without any pre-oxidation or surface modification treatment.
generation.boundary: The protective effect relies on the integrity and adhesion of the alumina scale; extreme thermal shocks, mechanical abrasion, or exposure to temperatures far exceeding the plating conditions may damage the oxide layer and diminish its corrosion protection. The improvement is expected only under conditions typical of hot-dip aluminum plating.
generation.uncertainty: The precise quantitative reduction in corrosion rate (e.g., the percent decrease in mass loss) and the optimum thickness or processing parameters for the alumina layer remain to be determined.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two groups of identical boride-based component specimens. Group A will receive the pre-oxidation treatment (heat in an oxygen‐rich atmosphere to form an Al2O3 layer), and Group B will remain untreated. Both groups will then be immersed in molten aluminum maintained at ~660°C for a fixed time period representative of typical hot-dip conditions. After exposure, the specimens will be cleaned and subjected to mass loss measurements, surface morphology analysis via SEM/EDS, and adhesion tests of any remaining surface layers.
measurements: SEM/EDS characterization of surface oxide layers and identification of corrosion products
Visual assessment and quantification of surface spallation or pitting
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the pre-oxidized (treated) specimens do not exhibit a statistically significant reduction in mass loss and surface corrosion damage compared to the untreated control group, or if the integrity of the alumina layer is not maintained after molten-aluminum exposure, the hypothesis will be considered falsified.

Corrosion resistance of alloys in light water reactors (LWRs) and more generally in oxidative environments is achieved by the formation of protective oxide layers that hinder further oxidation. Alloys containing Cr, Al, or Si typically tend to form a compact and self-healing chromia (Cr2O3), alumina (Al2O3) or silica (SiO2) layers, respectively, which acts as effective diffusion barriers against further oxidation. However, in molten fluoride salts (salt of choice for many molten salt reactor concepts, MSRs) these protective oxide layers on structural alloys are unstable which in turn leads to the dissolution of the least noble element in the alloy. Such a corrosion mechanism can lead to a reduction in components’ wall thickness and eventually the loss of the structural integrity of the reactor components,. The dissolution products themselves may lead to plate-out in the relatively cooler sections of the system due to the strong sensitivity of solubility of analytes to temperature.
